problem.summary: 点云中的三维物体检测是自动驾驶等机器人应用的关键任务。现有编码器存在速度与精度的权衡：固定编码器速度快但精度低，而从数据学习的编码器精度高但速度慢。

motivation.summary: 需要一种既能保持高精度又能实现高速推理的点云编码方法，以满足自动驾驶等实时应用的需求。

core_idea.summary: 提出PointPillars，一种新颖的编码器，利用PointNet学习垂直柱体（pillars）组织的点云表示。该编码器生成的特征可用于任何标准的2D卷积检测架构，并进一步提出了一个精简的下游网络。

method.summary: 1. 将点云组织成垂直柱体（pillars）。2. 使用简化的PointNet（线性层+BatchNorm+ReLU+最大池化）学习每个柱体的特征。3. 将特征散射回原始位置形成伪图像。4. 使用2D卷积骨干网络处理伪图像。5. 使用SSD检测头预测3D边界框。

experiments.summary: 在KITTI数据集上进行了广泛实验，包括BEV和3D检测基准测试。与多种现有方法（包括融合方法）进行了比较，并进行了消融研究以分析关键设计选择。

claims.claim: PointPillars在速度和精度上均大幅超越现有编码器。
仅使用激光雷达的完整检测管道显著优于现有技术，甚至包括融合方法。
在62Hz下运行，实现了2-4倍的运行时改进。
更快的版本在105Hz下匹配了现有技术的性能。
学习型编码器（如PointPillars）明显优于固定编码器。
结合地面真值数据库采样后，简单的每框增强策略效果更好。

limitations.limitation: 仅使用激光雷达，未利用图像信息。
在KITTI数据集上评估，可能在其他数据集或场景中表现不同。
某些实现细节（如具体的数据增强参数）可能需要针对新任务调整。

nodes.title: 点云到伪图像转换
nodes.label: 输入处理
nodes.summary: 将原始点云转换为适合2D卷积处理的伪图像表示。
nodes.description: 1. 将点云组织成垂直柱体（pillars）。2. 对每个点进行特征增强（添加到柱体中心的距离和偏移）。3. 创建密集张量（D, P, N）。4. 使用简化的PointNet学习特征。5. 将特征散射回原始位置形成伪图像（C, H, W）。

nodes.title: 骨干网络
nodes.label: 特征提取
nodes.summary: 使用2D卷积骨干网络处理伪图像，提取多尺度特征。
nodes.description: 骨干网络包含两个子网络：一个自上而下的网络生成越来越小的空间分辨率特征，另一个网络执行上采样和特征拼接。具体结构为Block1(S, 4, C), Block2(2S, 6, 2C), Block3(4S, 6, 4C)，以及对应的上采样步骤Up1, Up2, Up3，最终拼接得到6C特征。

nodes.title: 检测头
nodes.label: 预测
nodes.summary: 使用SSD检测头从骨干网络特征中预测3D边界框。
nodes.description: 检测头接收骨干网络输出的6C特征，预测物体的类别、位置、尺寸和方向。使用锚框匹配策略和非极大值抑制（NMS）生成最终检测结果。

nodes.title: 损失函数
nodes.label: 优化目标
nodes.summary: 定义并优化用于训练的多任务损失函数。
nodes.description: 损失函数包括定位损失（Lloc）、分类损失（Lcls，使用焦点损失）和方向损失（Ldir）。总损失为L = 1/Npos * (βloc*Lloc + βcls*Lcls + βdir*Ldir)，其中Npos为正锚框数量，βloc=2, βcls=1, βdir=0.2。

nodes.title: 数据增强
nodes.label: 训练技巧
nodes.summary: 使用关键的数据增强策略提升模型性能。
nodes.description: 1. 从地面真值数据库中采样物体并添加到当前点云中（汽车15个，行人0个，骑车人8个）。2. 对每个地面真值框进行旋转和平移增强。3. 对整个点云进行全局旋转和平移增强。

edges.label: 伪图像输入
edges.description: 点云到伪图像转换模块的输出作为骨干网络的输入。

edges.label: 特征图输入
edges.description: 骨干网络提取的多尺度特征图作为检测头的输入。

edges.label: 预测与损失计算
edges.description: 检测头的预测结果与地面真值一起用于计算损失函数。

edges.label: 增强点云
edges.description: 数据增强后的点云作为点云到伪图像转换模块的输入。

deltas.before: VoxelNet使用3D体素网格和3D卷积层处理点云，计算量大，推理速度慢（4.4Hz）。
deltas.after: PointPillars将点云组织成垂直柱体（pillars），使用简化的PointNet学习特征，然后散射形成伪图像，用2D卷积处理。
deltas.why_it_matters: 避免了昂贵的3D卷积，大幅提升了推理速度（62Hz vs 4.4Hz），同时保持了高精度。

deltas.before: VoxelNet等方法使用复杂的3D卷积骨干网络。
deltas.after: PointPillars使用精简的2D卷积骨干网络（类似SECOND的结构）和SSD检测头。
deltas.why_it_matters: 进一步简化了网络结构，提高了计算效率，同时利用了成熟的2D目标检测架构。

deltas.before: VoxelNet等方法需要复杂的3D卷积操作。
deltas.after: PointPillars的编码器（简化PointNet）可以高效实现为1x1卷积。
deltas.why_it_matters: 编码器计算效率极高，是整体速度提升的关键因素之一。

deltas.before: VoxelNet等方法使用复杂的每框数据增强策略。
deltas.after: PointPillars发现结合地面真值数据库采样后，简单的每框增强效果更好。
deltas.why_it_matters: 简化了训练流程，同时提升了性能（特别是对行人和骑车人）。

formulas.formula: \Delta x = \frac{x_{gt} - x_a}{d_a}, \quad \Delta y = \frac{y_{gt} - y_a}{d_a}, \quad \Delta z = \frac{z_{gt} - z_a}{h_a}

variables.name: x_{gt}, y_{gt}, z_{gt}
variables.description: 地面真值框的中心坐标

variables.name: d_a
variables.description: 锚框的对角线长度，d_a = \sqrt{w_a^2 + l_a^2}

formulas.intuition: 计算预测框与锚框在位置上的相对偏移，并进行归一化，使不同大小的锚框具有可比性。

variables.name: w_{gt}, l_{gt}, h_{gt}
variables.description: 地面真值框的宽度、长度、高度

formulas.intuition: 计算预测框与锚框在尺寸上的对数比值，便于优化。
使用正弦函数计算方向残差，以处理角度的周期性。
对所有定位参数（位置、尺寸、方向）的回归残差计算平滑L1损失。
使用焦点损失解决前景-背景类别不平衡问题，聚焦于难分类的样本。

variables.name: \beta_{loc}, \beta_{cls}, \beta_{dir}
variables.description: 各项损失的权重，分别为2, 1, 0.2

formulas.intuition: 将定位损失、分类损失和方向损失加权求和，并除以正锚框数量进行归一化。

main_result.description: 在KITTI测试集上的BEV和3D检测基准测试结果。
main_result.results: PointPillars在BEV和3D检测上均大幅超越所有仅使用激光雷达的方法，并优于大多数融合方法。在BEV mAP上达到62.58（所有类别），在3D mAP上达到55.62（所有类别）。

ablation.description: 对关键设计选择进行的消融研究。
ablation.results: 1. 空间分辨率：较小的柱体尺寸（0.16m）精度更高，但速度较慢；较大的柱体尺寸（0.28m）速度更快（105Hz），但精度略有下降。2. 数据增强：结合地面真值采样后，简单的每框增强效果更好。3. 点装饰：添加xp和yp偏移量可提升0.5 mAP。4. 编码器比较：学习型编码器（如PointPillars）明显优于固定编码器，尤其是在较大分辨率下。

robustness.description: 对不同物体类别和难度级别的性能分析。
robustness.results: 在汽车类别上表现最佳，在行人和骑车人上更具挑战性。常见失败模式包括对遮挡或远处物体的漏检，以及行人和骑车人之间的误分类。

scaling.description: 不同空间分辨率（柱体尺寸）对速度和精度的影响。
scaling.results: 柱体尺寸从0.16m增加到0.28m时，推理速度从62Hz提升到105Hz，但BEV mAP略有下降（主要由于行人和骑车人类别）。

case_study.description: 定性结果分析，包括成功和失败案例。
case_study.results: 成功案例：对汽车的检测准确，边界框紧密且方向正确。失败案例：1) 对部分遮挡或远处物体的漏检；2) 对类似类别（如货车、电车）的误检；3) 行人和骑车人之间的误分类；4) 某些情况下正确检测到了地面真值标注中缺失的物体。

benchmark.description: 在KITTI数据集上的标准基准测试。
benchmark.results: 在KITTI测试集的BEV和3D检测排行榜上，PointPillars在仅使用激光雷达的方法中排名第一，并优于大多数融合方法。在AOS（平均方向相似度）基准上也表现优异。

efficiency.description: 推理速度和运行时分析。
efficiency.results: PointPillars在桌面GPU（1080ti）上以62Hz运行，比VoxelNet（4.4Hz）快14倍，比SECOND（20Hz）快3倍。更快的版本（使用0.28m柱体尺寸）在105Hz下运行，匹配了现有技术的性能。

experiments.results: PointPillars在BEV和3D检测上均大幅超越所有仅使用激光雷达的方法，并优于大多数融合方法。在BEV mAP上达到62.58（所有类别），在3D mAP上达到55.62（所有类别）。

terms.definition: 本文提出的点云编码器，将点云组织成垂直柱体（pillars），并使用简化的PointNet学习特征。
垂直柱体，是PointPillars中组织点云的基本单元。点云被划分到XY平面上的网格中，每个网格单元（柱体）包含该垂直列中的所有点。
将柱体特征散射回原始网格位置后形成的2D特征图，可以被标准的2D卷积网络处理。
一种用于处理无序点集的神经网络架构。本文使用了简化的PointNet版本（线性层+BatchNorm+ReLU+最大池化）。
鸟瞰图，一种从正上方观察的视角。在3D物体检测中，BEV表示将3D点云投影到地面平面上形成的2D图像。
三维物体检测，目标是在3D空间中定位物体并预测其尺寸和方向。
一个广泛使用的自动驾驶计算机视觉算法评测数据集，包含激光雷达点云和图像数据。
预定义的参考框，用于与地面真值框匹配并计算回归残差。每个类别有多个不同尺寸和方向的锚框。
一种用于解决类别不平衡问题的损失函数，通过降低易分类样本的权重，使模型更关注难分类样本。
非极大值抑制，一种后处理技术，用于消除重叠的检测框，保留置信度最高的框。

required_models: PointPillars网络架构（Pillar Feature Net + 2D CNN Backbone + SSD Detection Head）
reproduction.required_compute: 桌面GPU（如NVIDIA 1080ti），训练时间未知，推理速度在1080ti上为62Hz（标准版本）或105Hz（快速版本）。

steps.description: 1. 数据准备：下载KITTI数据集，按照论文描述划分训练集、验证集和测试集。
2. 数据预处理：将点云组织成柱体，进行特征增强（添加xc, yc, zc, xp, yp）。
3. 模型构建：实现Pillar Feature Net（简化PointNet）、2D CNN骨干网络和SSD检测头。
4. 损失函数：实现定位损失（SmoothL1）、分类损失（Focal Loss）和方向损失（Softmax）。
5. 训练：使用Adam优化器，初始学习率2e-4，每15个epoch衰减0.8倍，训练160个epoch。使用数据增强（地面真值采样、每框增强、全局增强）。
6. 评估：在KITTI验证集和测试集上评估BEV和3D检测性能，使用官方评估指标。
7. 推理优化：调整柱体尺寸（如0.28m）以平衡速度和精度。

metadata.title: PointPillars: Fast Encoders for Object Detection From Point Clouds
metadata.paper_type: Computer Vision / Object Detection / Computer Vision / Pose Estimation / Computer Vision / CNN / Top-cited Computer Vision paper
metadata.abstract: Object detection in point clouds is an important aspect of many robotics applications such as autonomous driving. In this paper, we consider the problem of encoding a point cloud into a format appropriate for a downstream detection pipeline. Recent literature suggests two types of encoders; fixed encoders tend to be fast but sacrifice accuracy, while encoders that are learned from data are more accurate, but slower. In this work, we propose PointPillars, a novel encoder which utilizes PointNets to learn a representation of point clouds organized in vertical columns (pillars). While the encoded features can be used with any standard 2D convolutional detection architecture, we further propose a lean downstream network. Extensive experimentation shows that PointPillars outperforms previous encoders with respect to both speed and accuracy by a large margin. Despite only using lidar, our full detection pipeline significantly outperforms the state of the art, even among fusion methods, with respect to both the 3D and bird鈥檚 eye view KITTI benchmarks. This detection performance is achieved while running at 62 Hz: a 2 - 4 fold runtime improvement. A faster version of our method matches the state of the art at 105 Hz. These benchmarks suggest that PointPillars is an appropriate encoding for object detection in point clouds.

Abstract

Object detection in point clouds is an important aspect of many robotics applications such as autonomous driving. In this paper we consider the problem of encoding a point cloud into a format appropriate for a downstream detection pipeline. Recent literature suggests two types of encoders; ﬁxed encoders tend to be fast but sacriﬁce accuracy, while encoders that are learned from data are more accurate, but slower. In this work we propose PointPillars, a novel en- coder which utilizes PointNets to learn a representation of point clouds organized in vertical columns (pillars). While the encoded features can be used with any standard 2D con- volutional detection architecture, we further propose a lean downstream network. Extensive experimentation shows that PointPillars outperforms previous encoders with respect to
both speed and accuracy by a large margin. Despite only

using lidar, our full detection pipeline signiﬁcantly outper- forms the state of the art, even among fusion methods, with respect to both the 3D and bird’s eye view KITTI bench- marks. This detection performance is achieved while run- ning at 62Hz: a 2 - 4 fold runtime improvement. A faster version of our method matches the state of the art at 105 Hz. These benchmarks suggest that PointPillars is an appropri- ate encoding for object detection in point clouds. 1. Introduction Deploying autonomous vehicles (A Vs) in urban environ-
ments poses a difﬁcult technological challenge. Among
other tasks, A Vs need to detect and track moving objects such as vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists in realtime. To achieve this, autonomous vehicles rely on several sensors
out of which the lidar is arguably the most important. A

lidar uses a laser scanner to measure the distance to the environment, thus generating a sparse point cloud repre- sentation. methods for computer vision, a large body of literature has
investigated to what extent this technology could be applied

towards object detection from lidar point clouds [31, 29, 30, 11, 2, 21, 15, 28, 26, 25]. While there are many similarities between the modalities, there are two key differences: 1) the point cloud is a sparse representation, while an image is dense and 2) the point cloud is 3D, while the image is 2D. As a result object detection from point clouds does not triv- ially lend itself to standard image convolutional pipelines. Some early works focus on either using 3D convolu- 1 arXiv:1812.05784v2 [cs.LG] 7 May 2019

tions [3] or a projection of the point cloud into the image [14]. Recent methods tend to view the lidar point cloud from a bird’s eye view [2, 11, 31, 30]. This overhead per- spective offers several advantages such as lack of scale am- biguity and the near lack of occlusion. However, the bird’s eye view tends to be extremely sparse which makes direct application of convolutional neural networks impractical and inefﬁcient. A common workaround to this problem is to partition the ground plane into a regular grid, for example 10 x 10 cm, and then per- form a hand crafted feature encoding method on the points in each grid cell [2, 11, 26, 30]. However, such methods may be sub-optimal since the hard-coded feature extraction method may not generalize to new conﬁgurations without signiﬁcant engineering efforts. To address these issues, and building on the PointNet design developed by Qi et al. [22], V oxelNet [31] was one of the ﬁrst methods to truly do end- to-end learning in this domain. V...
only lidar point clouds, it dominates the current state of the

art including methods that use lidar and images, thus estab- lishing new standards for performance on both BEV and 3D detection (Table 1 and Table 2). At the same time PointPil- lars runs at 62Hz, which is orders of magnitude faster than previous art. PointPillars further enables a trade off between speed and accuracy; in one setting we match state of the art performance at over 100 Hz (Figure 5). We have also re- leased code (https://github.com/nutonomy/second.pytorch) that can reproduce our results. 1.1. Related Work We start by reviewing recent work in applying convolu- tional neural networks toward object detection in general, and then focus on methods speciﬁc to object detection from lidar point clouds.
1.1.1 Object detection using CNNs
Starting with the seminal work of Girshick et al. [6] it was

established that convolutional neural network (CNN) archi- tectures are state of the art for detection in images. The series of papers that followed [24, 7] advocate a two-stage approach to this problem, where in the ﬁrst stage a re- gion proposal network (RPN) suggests candidate proposals. Cropped and resized versions of these proposals are then classiﬁed by a second stage network. Two-stage methods
dominated the important vision benchmark datasets such as

COCO [17] over single-stage architectures originally pro- posed by Liu et al. [18]. In a single-stage architecture a dense set of anchor boxes is regressed and classiﬁed in a single stage into a set of predictions providing a fast and simple architecture. Recently Lin et al. [16] convincingly
argued that with their proposed focal loss function a sin-
gle stage method is superior to two-stage methods, both in terms of accuracyand runtime. In this work, we use a single stage method.
1.1.2 Object detection in lidar point clouds

Object detection in point clouds is an intrinsically three di- mensional problem. As such, it is natural to deploy a 3D convolutional network for detection, which is the paradigm of several early works [3, 13]. While providing a straight- forward architecture, these methods are slow; e.g. Engelcke et al. [3] require 0.5s for inference on a single point cloud. Most recent methods improve the runtime by projecting the 3D point cloud either onto the ground plane [11, 2] or the image plane [14]. In the most common paradigm the point cloud is organized in voxels and the set of voxels in each vertical column is encoded into a ﬁxed-length, hand- crafted, feature encoding to form a pseudo-image which can be processed by a standard image detection architecture. Some notable works here include MV3D [2], A VOD [11], PIXOR [30] and Complex YOLO [26] which all use varia- tions on the same ﬁxed encoding paradigm as the ﬁrst step of their architectures. The ﬁrst two methods additionally fuse the lid...

In their seminal work Qi et al. [22, 23] proposed a simple

architecture, PointNet, for learning from unordered point sets, which offered a path to full end-to-end learning. V ox- elNet [31] is one of the ﬁrst methods to deploy PointNets for object detection in lidar point clouds. In their method, PointNets are applied to voxels which are then processed by a set of 3D convolutional layers followed by a 2D backbone and a detection head. This enables end-to-end learning, but like the earlier work that relied on 3D convolutions, V oxel- Net is slow, requiring 225ms inference time ( 4.4Hz) for a single point cloud. Another recent method, Frustum Point- Net [21], uses PointNets to segment and classify the point cloud in a frustum generated from projecting a detection on an image into 3D. Frustum PointNet’s achieved high bench- mark performance compared to other fusion methods, but its multi-stage design makes end-to-end learning impracti- cal. factors that enable a strong detection performance. 2. PointPillars Network PointPillars accepts point clouds as input and estimates oriented 3D boxes for cars, pedestrians and cyclists. It con- sists of three main stages (Figure 2): (1) A feature encoder network that converts a point cloud to a sparse pseudo- image; (2) a 2D convolutional backbone to process the pseudo-image into high-level representation; and (3) a de- tection head that detects and regresses 3D boxes. 2.1. Pointcloud to Pseudo-Image To apply a 2D convolutional architecture, we ﬁrst con- vert the point cloud to a pseudo-image. We denote byl a point in a point cloud with coordinates x, y, z and reﬂectance r. As a ﬁrst step the point cloud is discretized into an evenly spaced grid in the x-y plane,
creating a set of pillarsP with|P| =B. Note that there is

no need for a hyper parameter to control the binning in the z dimension. The points in each pillar are then augmented with xc, yc, zc, xp and yp where the c subscript denotes distance to the arithmetic mean of all points in the pillar and thep subscript denotes the offset from the pillarx,y center.
The augmented lidar pointl is nowD = 9 dimensional.

The set of pillars will be mostly empty due to sparsity of the point cloud, and the non-empty pillars will in general have few points in them. For example, at 0.162 m2 bins the point cloud from an HDL-64E Velodyne lidar has 6k-9k non-empty pillars in the range typically used in KITTI for ∼ 97% sparsity. This sparsity is exploited by imposing a limit both on the number of non-empty pillars per sample (P ) and on the number of points per pillar ( N) to create a dense tensor of size (D,P,N ). If a sample or pillar holds too much data to ﬁt in this tensor the data is randomly sam- pled. Conversely, if a sample or pillar has too little data to populate the tensor, zero padding is applied.

3. Implementation Details In this section we describe our network parameters and the loss function that we optimize for.
3.1. Network Instead of pre-training our networks, all weights were initialized randomly using a uniform distribution as in [8].
The encoder network has C = 64 output features. The
car and pedestrian/cyclist backbones are the same except
for the stride of the ﬁrst block ( S = 2 for car, S = 1 for

pedestrian/cyclist). Both network consists of three blocks, Block1(S, 4, C), Block2( 2S, 6, 2C), and Block3( 4S, 6, 4C). To optimize the loss function we use the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 2∗ 10−4 and decay the learn- ing rate by a factor of 0.8 every 15 epochs and train for 160 epochs. We use a batch size of 2 for validation set and 4 for our test submission. 4. Experimental setup In this section we present our experimental setup, includ- ing dataset, experimental settings and data augmentation. 4.1. Dataset All experiments use the KITTI object detection bench- mark dataset [5], which consists of samples that have both lidar point clouds and images. We only train on lidar point clouds, but compare with fusion methods that use both lidar and images. The samples are originally divided into 7481 training and 7518 testing samples. For experimental studies we split the ofﬁcial training into 3712 training samples and 3769 validation samples [1], while for our test submission
we created a minival set of 784 samples from the valida-

tion set and trained on the remaining 6733 samples. The KITTI benchmark requires detections of cars, pedestrians, and cyclists. Since the ground truth objects were only anno- tated if they are visible in the image, we follow the standard convention [2, 31] of only using lidar points that project into the image. Following the standard literature practice on KITTI [11, 31, 28], we train one network for cars and one network for both pedestrians and cyclists. 4.2. Settings Unless explicitly varied in an experimental study, we use
an xy resolution: 0.16 m, max number of pillars (P ): 12000,
and max number of points per pillar (N): 100.

We use the same anchors and matching strategy as [31]. Each class anchor is described by a width, length, height, and z center, and is applied at two orientations: 0 and 90 degrees. Anchors are matched to ground truth using the 2D IoU with the following rules. A positive match is either the highest with a ground truth box, or above the positive match threshold, while a negative match is below the nega- tive threshold. All other anchors are ignored in the loss.
At inference time we apply axis aligned non maximum

suppression (NMS) with an overlap threshold of 0.5 IoU. This provides similar performance compared to rotational NMS, but is much faster. Car . The x, y, z range is [(0, 70.4), (-40, 40), (-3, 1)] meters respectively. The car anchor has width, length, and height of (1.6, 3.9, 1.5) m with a z center of -1 m. 4.3. Data Augmentation Data augmentation is critical for good performance on the KITTI benchmark [28, 30, 2]. First, following SECOND [28], we create a lookup table of the ground truth 3D boxes for all classes and the asso- ciated point clouds that falls inside these 3D boxes. Then for each sample, we randomly select 15, 0, 8 ground truth samples for cars, pedestrians, and cyclists respectively and place them into the current point cloud. We found these settings to perform better than the proposed settings [28]. Next, all ground truth boxes are individually augmented. Each box is rotated (uniformly drawn from [−π/20,π/ 20]) and translated (x, y, and z independently drawn from N (0, 0.25)) to further enrich the training set. Finally, we perform two sets of global augmentations that are jointly applied to the point cloud and all boxes. First, we apply random mirroring ﬂip along the x axis [30], then a global rotation and scaling [31, 28]. Finally, we ap- ply a global translation with x,...

The performance of PointPillars on AOS signiﬁcantly ex- ceeds in all strata as compared to the only two 3D detection methods [11, 28] that predict oriented boxes (Table 3). In general, image only methods perform best on 2D detection since the 3D projection of boxes into the image can result in loose boxes depending on the 3D pose. Despite this, Point- Pillars moderate cyclist AOS of 68.16 outperforms the best image based method [27]. For comparison to other methods on val, we note that our network achieved BEV AP of (87.98, 63.55, 69.71) and 3D AP of (77.98, 57.86, 66.02) for the moderate strata of cars, pedestrians, and cyclists respectively.

Realtime Inference As indicated by our results (Table 1 and Figure 5), Point- Pillars represent a signiﬁcant improvement in terms of in- ference runtime. In this section we break down our run- time and consider the different design choices that enabled this speedup. We focus on the car network, but the pedes- trian and bicycle network runs at a similar speed since the smaller range cancels the effect of the backbone operating at lower strides. All runtimes are measured on a desktop with an Intel i7 CPU and a 1080ti GPU. The main inference steps are as follows. First, the point cloud is loaded and ﬁltered based on range and visibility in the images (1.4ms). Then, the points are organized in pil- lars and decorated (2.7ms). Next, the PointPillar tensor is uploaded to the GPU (2.9ms), encoded (1.3ms), scattered to the pseudo-image ( 0.1ms), and processed by the back- bone and detection heads (7.7ms). Finally NMS is applied o...

However, an operational A V needs to view the full environment and process the complete point cloud, signif- icantly increasing all aspects of the runtime. Second, tim- ing measurements in the literature are typically done on a high-power desktop GPU. However, an operational A V may instead use embedded GPUs or embedded compute which may not have the same throughput. 7. Per Box Data Augmentation Both V oxelNet [31] and SECOND [28] recommend ex- tensive per box augmentation. However, in our experi-

First, despite notes in the original papers that their encoder only works on cars, we found that the MV3D [2] and PIXOR [30] en- coders can learn pedestrians and cyclists quite well. Second, our implementations beat the respective published results
by a large margin ( 1− 10 mAP). While this is not an ap-

ples to apples comparison since we only used the respective encoders and not the full network architectures, the perfor- mance difference is noteworthy. We see several potential reasons. For V oxelNet and SECOND we suspect the boost in performance comes from improved data augmentation hyperparameters as discussed in Section 7.2. Among the ﬁxed encoders, roughly half the performance increase can be explained by the introduction of ground truth database sampling [28], which we found to boost the mAP by around 3% mAP. The remaining differences are likely due to a com- bination of multiple hyperparameters including network de- sign (number of layers, type of layers, whether to use a fea- ture pyramid); anchor box design (or lack thereof [30]); lo- calization loss with respect to 3D and angle; classiﬁcation loss; optimizer choices (SGD vs Adam, batch size); and more. However, a more careful study is needed to isolate each cause and effect. 8. Conclusion In this paper, we introduce PointPil...
